extracted.intended_audience: general readers, students and researchers of art history and avant-garde movements
extracted.subtask_description: Guidance and descriptive criteria for producing and assessing Surrealist works across media (painting, literature, film, theatre, photography, music) as presented in an encyclopedic overview of the movement.

rubrics_metrics.name: Pure psychic automatism / allow unconscious expression
rubrics_metrics.description: Surrealism is defined (Breton, dictionary) as 'pure psychic automatism, by which one proposes to express, either verbally, in writing, or by any other manner, the real functioning of thought. Dictation of thought in the absence of all control exercised by reason, outside of all aesthetic and moral preoccupation.'
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Techniques: automatic writing and automatic drawing are central methods; artists and writers attempted to 'dictate' thought without rational censorship. Note: the article also observes that much 'automatic' material was later edited and 'very thought out', so absolute spontaneity is an ideal rather than an invariant practice.

rubrics_metrics.name: Element of surprise, unexpected juxtapositions and non sequitur
rubrics_metrics.description: Works of Surrealism 'feature the element of surprise, unexpected juxtapositions and non sequitur.'
rubrics_metrics.guidance: This aesthetic principle applies across media (painting, writing, photography, film, comedy). Use of surprising pairings and illogical sequences is a core criterion for evaluating surreality. Anti-pattern: reliance on literal, conventional, or purely rational arrangement that avoids surprise.

rubrics_metrics.name: Startling juxtapositions: distance between realities increases image strength
rubrics_metrics.description: Quoted from Pierre Reverdy and cited by Breton: 'a juxtaposition of two more or less distant realities. The more the relationship between the two juxtaposed realities is distant and true, the stronger the image will be−the greater its emotional power and poetic reality.'
rubrics_metrics.guidance: When combining elements, greater conceptual/associative distance (if convincingly held together) tends to increase emotional/poetic impact. Practical implication: seek combinations that are unexpectedly remote but produce a 'true' associative resonance rather than arbitrary collage.

rubrics_metrics.name: Resolve dream and reality into an 'absolute reality' (surreality)
rubrics_metrics.description: Breton's stated intention: to 'resolve the previously contradictory conditions of dream and reality into an absolute reality, a super-reality', or surreality.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Effective Surrealist work often blends dream logic and waking reality so that the resulting work functions as a new, coherent 'super-reality.' Assess works by how convincingly and provocatively they merge dream and ordinary experience.

rubrics_metrics.name: Techniques of automatism and specific pictorial methods
rubrics_metrics.description: Surrealists developed and used techniques such as automatic writing, automatic drawing, frottage, grattage, decalcomania, photomontage, collage, fumage, coulage and other chance-based pictorial procedures.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Use of these named methods (and inventing analogous methods) is a hallmark of Surrealist practice, especially for generating unexpected forms and content. Examples: André Masson's automatic drawings, Max Ernst's collages, Paalen's fumage. Inclusion of such techniques is a positive production/evaluation signal; absence does not preclude Surrealist affinity but changes method.

rubrics_metrics.name: Emphasis on dream analysis and Freudian methods to access the unconscious
rubrics_metrics.description: The movement drew heavily on Freud's concepts of free association and dream analysis; Breton used psychoanalytic methods in clinical contexts and Surrealists used these ideas to 'liberate the imagination.'
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Works that exploit dream logic, symbolic imagery, free association, and unconscious material align with Surrealist aims. Evaluators may look for evidence of dream-derived imagery, symbolic condensation, or associative chains indicative of unconscious material.

rubrics_metrics.name: Disdain for literal meanings; focus on connotations, undertones and poetic undercurrents
rubrics_metrics.description: Surrealist literature and publications 'showed their disdain for literal meanings given to objects and focused rather on the undertones; the poetic undercurrents present.'
rubrics_metrics.guidance: In textual work, value is placed on evocative connotation, ambiguous relationships to visual images, dream-accounts, and associative logic rather than straightforward narrative exposition. Anti-pattern: didactic literalism or overemphasis on explicit, didactic meaning.

rubrics_metrics.name: Convulsive joining as a tool for revelation
rubrics_metrics.description: Magritte and others used the 'convulsive joining' (startling juxtapositions) as 'a tool for revelation in and of itself.'
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Assess whether abrupt or violent juxtaposition yields insight or new perception rather than mere shock. Judicious 'convulsive' combination that reveals psychological or poetic truth is a Surrealist aim.

rubrics_metrics.name: Expose psychological truth by stripping ordinary objects of normal significance
rubrics_metrics.description: Surrealism as a visual movement 'had found a method: to expose psychological truth; stripping ordinary objects of their normal significance, to create a compelling image that was beyond ordinary formal organization, in order to evoke empathy from the viewer.'
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Evaluation criteria for visual works: are everyday objects recontextualized to foreground unconscious associations or psychological content? Success judged by the work's ability to evoke affect and to transcend formal conventionality.

rubrics_metrics.name: Openness to flux and continual reinvention of methods and philosophy
rubrics_metrics.description: Surrealism 'was meant to be always in flux—to be more modern than modern—and so it was natural there should be a rapid shuffling of the philosophy as new challenges arose.'
rubrics_metrics.guidance: A Surrealist approach welcomes methodological experimentation and changes in theory; rigid dogma or strict orthodoxy is contrary to the movement's self-characterization. Works are assessed for imaginative innovation and willingness to evolve techniques and aims.

rubrics_metrics.name: Political/revolutionary engagement as part of Surrealist praxis
rubrics_metrics.description: Breton was explicit that Surrealism was 'above all, a revolutionary movement.' The movement aligned at times with communism, Trotskyism, anarchism, and other radical politics.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: For many Surrealists, political commitment and the desire to change social conditions were central. Evaluation of historical or political Surrealist projects may consider whether art and political praxis are integrated and whether the work furthers revolutionary critique; note that political alignment varied and produced schisms.

rubrics_metrics.name: Application across media with medium-specific criteria (film, theatre, music, photography)
rubrics_metrics.description: Surrealist principles were applied in cinema, theatre, music, photography and other media; each medium developed its own practices (e.g., Surrealist cinema such as Un Chien Andalou; theatre emphasizing physical ritual and the Theatre of Cruelty; music employing improvisation or dream-derived sequences).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: When evaluating Surrealism in a specific medium, apply the general Surrealist criteria (automatism, juxtapositions, dream logic) while attending to medium-specific tactics: film montage and shocking sequences, theatrical physicality and non-verbal ritual, photographic uncanny compositions, musical improvisation or aleatoric structures.

rubrics_metrics.name: Exhibition and performative acts as creative Surrealist statements
rubrics_metrics.description: Surrealists treated exhibitions and installations as creative acts (e.g., Exposition Internationale du Surréalisme with immersive environments, Rainy Taxi, Surrealist Street), designing scenography and experiences to scandalize and provoke the viewer.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Assessments of Surrealist exhibitions should consider whether the exhibition design itself performs Surrealist aims (provocation, recontextualization, sensory disturbance) rather than merely displaying objects.

rubrics_metrics.name: Use of chance, anti-art tactics and Dadaist inheritance
rubrics_metrics.description: Surrealism grew out of and was influenced by Dada and anti-art practices; chance operations, anti-bourgeois provocations and performance elements feature in Surrealist practice.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Works employing chance procedures, subversive stunts, or anti-art gestures align with Surrealist lineage. However, Surrealists often distinguished their project from Dada by emphasizing automatism and revolutionary aims rather than pure nihilism.
